hints: Look at what this reaction really is, burning a hydrocarbon fragment in $\text{NO}_2$ to make $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. What do you know about combustion type reactions?
Notice the products $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ are very stable compounds with large negative standard enthalpies of formation.
Remember that bond breaking needs energy in while bond making and forming stable products releases lots of energy out, so decide which effect wins here.
walkthrough:
**Decide if this is exothermic or endothermic**

Think of this like combustion. A fuel fragment $\text{CH}_3\bullet$ is oxidised to $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Combustion reactions are famously exothermic because very stable products are made:
$$4\text{CH}_3\bullet + 7\text{NO}_2 \rightarrow 3\frac{1}{2}\text{N}_2 + 4\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Use enthalpy of formation thinking**

Enthalpy change can be estimated from:
$$\Delta H_r^\ominus = \sum \Delta H_f^\ominus(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H_f^\ominus(\text{reactants})$$
$\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ have large negative $\Delta H_f^\ominus$ values, meaning a lot of energy is released when they form from elements.

**Check bond energy thinking**

Breaking bonds, such as N-O double bonds in $\text{NO}_2$, always requires energy in, so it is endothermic. Making new strong bonds, such as C=O in $\text{CO}_2$, O-H in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and N triple N in $\text{N}_2$, releases energy out.

Here the energy released on making the very stable products far outweighs the energy taken in to break reactants, so overall $\Delta H$ is negative and exothermic.

options.A: Incorrect. The reaction is exothermic, not endothermic. Also, converting chemical energy to heat energy describes what happens in an exothermic reaction, not a reason for an endothermic one.
options.B: Incorrect. The reaction is exothermic, not endothermic. A very high N triple N bond energy means a lot of energy is released when $\text{N}_2$ is formed, which would favour an exothermic change, not cause an endothermic one.
options.C: Correct. The reaction is exothermic because the products $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ are very stable with large negative $\Delta H_f^\ominus$ values. Forming them releases much more energy than is needed to break the reactant bonds.
options.D: Incorrect reason. The reaction is exothermic, but breaking double bonds in $\text{NO}_2$ requires energy in and is endothermic. Bond breaking alone can never be the reason a reaction is exothermic.
